blocks.text: Whenever work is done on a body it increases its energy. For example, if a force F acts on a body of mass m, initially moving with velocity vi, through a distance d and increases its velocity to vf, the acceleration produced is given by 2ad = vf^2 - vi^2, or a = (vf^2 - vi^2)/(2d) ... (4.16). From the second law of motion F = ma, or a = F/m ... (4.17). Comparing Eqs. 4.16 and 4.17, F/m = (vf^2 - vi^2)/(2d), or F d = (1/2) m vf^2 - (1/2) m vi^2 ... (4.18). This expression is the work-energy theorem.

blocks.title: Work-energy theorem
blocks.text: The change in kinetic energy of an object is equal to the work done on it by a net force: W = change in kinetic energy = (KE)f - (KE)i = (1/2) m vf^2 - (1/2) m vi^2. This is also known as the work-energy principle.

The work-energy theorem is applicable for any direction of the force relative to the displacement. For instance, an object with kinetic energy can perform work if it is allowed to push or pull on another object; in this case the work is taken as negative and the kinetic energy of the object decreases. The theorem remains valid even if the force varies from point to point.

blocks.title: Example 4.4
blocks.text: A motorcycle rider weighing 60 kg coasts down a 24-degree slope; the motorcycle weighs 30 kg. At the top of the slope the speed is 3.2 m s^-1. If the kinetic frictional force is 100 N, what is the speed 72 m downhill? Solution: the normal force F_N is balanced by the component of the weight (mg cos 24) perpendicular to the slope. With kinetic frictional force f, the net force F is F = mg sin 24 - f, where m = total mass = 60 kg + 30 kg = 90 kg: F = (90 kg x 9.8 m s^-2 x 0.4) - 100 N = 252.8 N. Work done W = F d = 252.8 N x 72 m = 18201.6 J. As the work is positive, applying the work-energy theorem W = (KE)f - (KE)i, (KE)f = W + (KE)i: (1/2) m vf^2 = W + (1/2) m vi^2, (1/2) x 90 kg x vf^2 = 18201 J + (1/2) x 90 kg x (3.2 m s^-1)^2. This gives vf^2 = 414.7 m^2 s^-2, or vf = sqrt(414.7) = 20.4 m s^-1.
All the food you eat in one day has about the same energy as 1/3 litre of petrol (Tid-bits).
